claim: Central amygdala neurons expressing protein kinase C-delta (CeA-PKCδ) are sensitized following nerve injury in mice.
source: Central amygdala neurons expressing protein kinase C-delta (CeA-PKCδ) are sensitized following nerve injury and promote pain-related responses in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that provides context for the study.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons promote pain-related responses in mice.
source: Central amygdala neurons expressing protein kinase C-delta (CeA-PKCδ) are sensitized following nerve injury and promote pain-related responses in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons project to the ventral region of the zona incerta (ZI).
source: In this study, we identified a neural circuit that originates in CeA-PKCδ neurons and terminates in the ventral region of the zona incerta (ZI), a subthalamic structure previously linked to pain processing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical tracing data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The zona incerta is a subthalamic structure previously linked to pain processing.
source: In this study, we identified a neural circuit that originates in CeA-PKCδ neurons and terminates in the ventral region of the zona incerta (ZI), a subthalamic structure previously linked to pain processing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior literature.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of GABAergic ZI neurons induced bilateral hypersensitivity in uninjured mice.
source: Behavioral experiments show that chemogenetic inhibition of GABAergic ZI neurons induced bilateral hypersensitivity in uninjured mice and contralateral hypersensitivity after nerve injury.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 3.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of GABAergic ZI neurons induced contralateral hypersensitivity after nerve injury.
source: Behavioral experiments show that chemogenetic inhibition of GABAergic ZI neurons induced bilateral hypersensitivity in uninjured mice and contralateral hypersensitivity after nerve injury.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 3.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of GABAergic ZI neurons reversed nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity.
source: In contrast, chemogenetic activation of GABAergic ZI neurons reversed nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ axonal terminals in the ZI reduces nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity.
source: Optogenetic manipulations of CeA-PKCδ axonal terminals in the ZI further showed that inhibition of this pathway reduces nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity whereas activation of the pathway produces hypersensitivity in the uninjured paws.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic behavioral data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ axonal terminals in the ZI produces hypersensitivity in the uninjured paws.
source: Optogenetic manipulations of CeA-PKCδ axonal terminals in the ZI further showed that inhibition of this pathway reduces nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity whereas activation of the pathway produces hypersensitivity in the uninjured paws.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic behavioral data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The pathway from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI is an inhibitory efferent pathway.
source: Altogether, our results identify a novel nociceptive inhibitory efferent pathway from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI that bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors in mice.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 2.

claim: The CeA-PKCδ to ZI pathway bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors in mice.
source: Altogether, our results identify a novel nociceptive inhibitory efferent pathway from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI that bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors in mice.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figures 3-8.

claim: Persistent pain resulting from lesions or diseases affecting the peripheral and central nervous systems can severely affect a person's life over time if left untreated.
source: Persistent pain resulting from lesions or diseases affecting the peripheral and central nervous systems can severely affect a person's life over time if left untreated (Dworkin, 2002; Treede et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The amygdala is a key locus in persistent pain processing.
source: Several neuroimaging, pharmacological and electrophysiological studies in humans and animals demonstrate that the amygdala is a key locus in persistent pain processing (Bernard and Besson, 1990; Bushnell et al., 2013; Carrasquillo and Gereau, 2007; Neugebauer et al., 2004; Zald, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The central nucleus of amygdala (CeA) can both enhance and decrease pain-related behaviors in a cell-type-specific manner.
source: A recent study further demonstrated that the central nucleus of amygdala (CeA) can both enhance and decrease pain-related behaviors in a cell-type-specific manner (Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CeA neurons expressing somatostatin are inhibited by nerve injury and promote decreases in pain-related behaviors.
source: In contrast, neurons expressing somatostatin are inhibited by nerve injury and promote decreases in pain-related behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: The ZI is a subthalamic nucleus located ventrolateral to the medial lemniscus and dorsomedial to the substantia nigra.
source: The ZI is a subthalamic nucleus located ventrolateral to the medial lemniscus and dorsomedial to the substantia nigra (Ricardo, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The ZI is comprised of heterogeneous groups of cells defined by the expression of molecular markers such as parvalbumin, tyrosine hydroxylase, somatostatin, calbindin, and glutamate.
source: The ZI is comprised of heterogeneous groups of cells defined by the expression of molecular markers such as parvalbumin, tyrosine hydroxylase, somatostatin, calbindin, and glutamate (Mitrofanis, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The ZI receives inputs from the CeA.
source: Previous studies using traditional anatomical tracing have shown that the ZI receives inputs from the CeA (Reardon and Mitrofanis, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing CeA neurons project to parvalbumin-expressing ZI neurons and contribute to conditioned fear memory.
source: A recent study further demonstrated that somatostatin-expressing CeA neurons project to parvalbumin-expressing ZI neurons and contribute to conditioned fear memory (Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The ZI modulates fear generalization in rodents.
source: The ZI has also been shown to modulate fear generalization (Venkataraman et al., 2019), binge eating (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017), defensive behaviors (Chou et al., 2018) and predatory hunting Zhao et al., 2019 in rodents, highlighting the functional complexity of this subthalamic brain structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The ZI modulates binge eating in rodents.
source: The ZI has also been shown to modulate fear generalization (Venkataraman et al., 2019), binge eating (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017), defensive behaviors (Chou et al., 2018) and predatory hunting Zhao et al., 2019 in rodents, highlighting the functional complexity of this subthalamic brain structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The ZI modulates defensive behaviors in rodents.
source: The ZI has also been shown to modulate fear generalization (Venkataraman et al., 2019), binge eating (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017), defensive behaviors (Chou et al., 2018) and predatory hunting Zhao et al., 2019 in rodents, highlighting the functional complexity of this subthalamic brain structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The ZI modulates predatory hunting in rodents.
source: The ZI has also been shown to modulate fear generalization (Venkataraman et al., 2019), binge eating (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017), defensive behaviors (Chou et al., 2018) and predatory hunting Zhao et al., 2019 in rodents, highlighting the functional complexity of this subthalamic brain structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Changes in neural activity have been reported in the ZI in rodent models of pain.
source: In rodent models of pain, changes in neural activity have been reported in the ZI (Masri et al., 2009) and behavioral studies further show that experimentally modulating the activity of ZI neurons alters behavioral hypersensitivity (Hu et al., 2019; Moon et al., 2016; Petronilho et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Experimentally modulating the activity of ZI neurons alters behavioral hypersensitivity.
source: In rodent models of pain, changes in neural activity have been reported in the ZI (Masri et al., 2009) and behavioral studies further show that experimentally modulating the activity of ZI neurons alters behavioral hypersensitivity (Hu et al., 2019; Moon et al., 2016; Petronilho et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Most of the literature suggests that the ZI is inhibited in the context of pain and that this inhibition drives behavioral hypersensitivity.
source: Most of the literature suggests that the ZI is inhibited in the context of pain and that this inhibition drives behavioral hypersensitivity (Hu et al., 2019; Masri et al., 2009; Moon et al., 2016; Moon and Park, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Deep brain stimulation of zona incerta reduced experimental heat pain in humans.
source: Consistent with this model, a recent study in humans showed that deep brain stimulation of zona incerta reduced experimental heat pain (Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Some studies report that the ZI is activated in the context of pain and these increases in neuronal activity drive hypersensitivity.
source: Previous studies in rodents, however, reports the opposite – the ZI is activated in the context of pain and these increases in neuronal activity drive hypersensitivity (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons are GABAergic.
source: Based on our anatomical findings demonstrating projections from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI, in combination with previous work showing that CeA-PKCδ neurons are GABAergic and display increases in activity following injury, we hypothesized that inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons are a source of pain-related inhibition in the ZI that results in increases in pain-related behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from previous work.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons display increases in activity following injury.
source: Based on our anatomical findings demonstrating projections from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI, in combination with previous work showing that CeA-PKCδ neurons are GABAergic and display increases in activity following injury, we hypothesized that inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons are a source of pain-related inhibition in the ZI that results in increases in pain-related behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information from previous work.

claim: AAV-DIO-mCherry was transduced in CeA-PKCδ cells as confirmed by immunostaining for PKCδ.
source: We confirmed transduction of mCherry in CeA-PKCδ cells with immunostaining for PKCδ (Figure 1B) and subsequently analyzed the anatomical localization of mCherry-positive axonal terminals throughout the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CeA-PKCδ efferent projections were found in 18 brain regions, including the basal forebrain, striatum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla.
source: These analyses revealed CeA-PKCδ efferent projections in 18 brain regions, including the basal forebrain, striatum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: The anatomical distributions and terminal densities observed in mice injected with ChrimsonR-tdTomato were comparable to those observed in mice injected with mCherry.
source: As summarized in Table 1, the anatomical distributions and terminal densities observed in mice injected with ChrimsonR-tdTomato were also comparable to those observed in mice injected with mCherry, showing that the identified regions are not dependent on the experimental approach used.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: Transduction was selectively localized to the CeA.
source: In addition, mapping and quantification of transduced cells showed that transduction was selectively localized to the CeA, and that transduction efficiency was robust and comparable with both approaches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Transduction efficiency was robust and comparable with both mCherry and ChrimsonR-tdTomato approaches.
source: In addition, mapping and quantification of transduced cells showed that transduction was selectively localized to the CeA, and that transduction efficiency was robust and comparable with both approaches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Axonal terminals in the output regions of CeA-PKCδ neurons have different terminal densities and organization patterns.
source: Semi-quantitative analysis, performed by visual examination of high magnification images, further revealed that axonal terminals in the output regions of CeA-PKCδ neurons have different terminal densities and organization patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on semi-quantitative analysis.

claim: Most of the brain regions identified had either few or moderate numbers of terminals.
source: Most of the brain regions identified had either few or moderate numbers of terminals, with only three regions, including the bed nucleus of stria terminalis, extended amygdala, and parabrachial nucleus, containing high densities of labeling (Figure 1C–D and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C-D and Table 1.

claim: Only three regions, including the bed nucleus of stria terminalis, extended amygdala, and parabrachial nucleus, contained high densities of labeling.
source: Most of the brain regions identified had either few or moderate numbers of terminals, with only three regions, including the bed nucleus of stria terminalis, extended amygdala, and parabrachial nucleus, containing high densities of labeling (Figure 1C–D and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C-D and Table 1.

claim: No terminal labeling was observed in cortical regions of any of the five brains evaluated.
source: Consistent with previous studies using traditional anterograde tracers in the CeA (Aggleton, 2000; Barbier et al., 2017; Reardon and Mitrofanis, 2000; Shinonaga et al., 1992; Zhou et al., 2018), no terminal labeling was observed in cortical regions of any of the five brains evaluated.
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Moderate CeA-PKCδ axonal terminal labeling was observed between rostral-caudal levels 1.46 mm and 2.70 mm posterior to bregma in the ZI.
source: As illustrated in the representative images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, moderate CeA-PKCδ axonal terminal labeling was observed between rostral-caudal levels 1.46 mm and 2.70 mm posterior to bregma.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CeA-PKCδ terminals were restricted to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI in all brains analyzed.
source: Mapping of the distribution of CeA-PKCδ terminals within the ZI further showed that these axonal terminals were restricted to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI in all brains analyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: CTB-647 was detected in CeA-PKCδ neurons, validating the anatomical projection from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI.
source: Notably, CTB-647 was detected in CeA-PKCδ neurons (Figure 2B), validating the anatomical projection from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Approximately 19% of CTB-positive CeA neurons are also positive for PKCδ-tdTomato.
source: Quantification of CeA neurons positive for both CTB-647 and PKCδ-tdTomato further revealed that approximately 19% of CTB-positive CeA neurons are also positive for PKCδ-tdTomato.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on quantification.

claim: Neurons positive for both CTB-647 and PKCδ-tdTomato were limited to the capsular and lateral subdivisions of the CeA.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, neurons positive for both CTB-647 and PKCδ-tdTomato were limited to the capsular and lateral subdivisions of the CeA, with higher densities observed in the middle/posterior regions of the CeA, between rostral-caudal levels 1.34 and 1.70 posterior to bregma.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons in the capsular and lateral CeA send inputs with moderate densities of terminals to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI.
source: Together, the results from our anatomical experiments show that CeA-PKCδ neurons in the capsular and lateral CeA send inputs with moderate densities of terminals to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on anatomical data.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals in the ZI showed robust inhibitory post-synaptic currents in 60% of VGAT-positive cells.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals in the ZI with blue light further showed robust inhibitory post-synaptic currents in 60% of VGAT-positive cells (12 out of 20 cells; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Optically evoked postsynaptic responses occurred in the presence of TTX and 4-AP, demonstrating that the inputs from the CeA to the ZI are monosynaptic.
source: Optically evoked postsynaptic responses occurred in the presence of TTX and 4-AP, demonstrating that the inputs from the CeA to the ZI are monosynaptic.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on electrophysiological data.

claim: 53% of VGAT-negative ZI neurons display inhibitory post-synaptic currents in response to optical stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals.
source: Of note, recordings in VGAT-negative ZI neurons revealed that 53% (8 out of 15 cells) of these ZI neurons also display inhibitory post-synaptic currents in response to optical stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on electrophysiological data.

claim: Paired pulse ratio is indistinguishable between VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons, demonstrating that CeA-synaptic inputs are comparable in VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons.
source: Quantification of the responses to optical paired stimulation further showed that paired pulse ratio is indistinguishable between VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons, demonstrating that CeA-synaptic inputs are comparable in VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The mean oIPSC amplitude in response to blue light stimulation was reduced after bath exchange to 10 µM bicuculline.
source: As illustrated in the representative traces and graph in Figure 2E, the mean oIPSC amplitude in response to blue light stimulation (470 nm, 10 mW) was reduced after bath exchange to 10 µM bicuculline.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Recordings at a holding potential of –70 mV showed either no response to blue light stimulation or a small inward current in neurons that showed robust light-evoked outward currents at holding potential of 0 mV.
source: Parallel recordings at a holding potential of –70 mV (near reversal potential for chloride) further showed either no response to blue light stimulation or a small inward current in neurons that showed robust light-evoked outward currents at holding potential of 0 mV (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The projection from the CeA to the ZI is inhibitory.
source: Together, these findings confirm that the projection from the CeA to the ZI is inhibitory.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on electrophysiological data.

claim: Bath application of CNO significantly inhibited firing responses in hM4Di-transduced neurons.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3A, bath application of the DREADD ligand clozapine N-oxide (CNO; 10 µM) significantly inhibited firing responses in hM4Di-transduced neurons, with no measurable effect observed in response to bath application of the saline vehicle control.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transduction of hM4Di was restricted to the ZI.
source: Histological verification of injection sites at the end of the experiments further demonstrated that transduction of hM4Di was restricted to the ZI (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of transduced cells within the ZI of mice stereotaxically injected with hM4Di was comparable to the numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of VGAT-positive cells in the ZI of VGAT-cre::Ai9 mice, demonstrating robust transduction efficiency.
source: The numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of transduced cells within the ZI of mice stereotaxically injected with hM4Di was comparable to the numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of VGAT-positive cells in the ZI of VGAT-cre::Ai9 mice, demonstrating robust transduction efficiency (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Following cuff implantation on the sciatic nerve, tactile and pressure sensitivity was significantly lower in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation compared to the contralateral hindpaw or either hindpaw in sham treated mice.
source: As expected, following cuff implantation on the sciatic nerve, tactile and pressure sensitivity was significantly lower in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation compared to the contralateral hindpaw or either hindpaw in sham treated mice (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in robust bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation in sham mice.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3E and F, chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in robust bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation in sham mice as well as contralateral hypersensitivity in cuff-implanted mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in contralateral hypersensitivity in cuff-implanted mice.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3E and F, chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in robust bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation in sham mice as well as contralateral hypersensitivity in cuff-implanted mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Withdrawal thresholds in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff treatment were indistinguishable before and after chemogenetic inactivation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons.
source: Withdrawal thresholds in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff treatment were indistinguishable before and after chemogenetic inactivation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons, demonstrating that inhibition of ZI cells does not measurably affect cuff-induced hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Inhibition of ZI VGAT-positive neurons is sufficient to elicit hypersensitivity in the absence of injury that resembles the hypersensitivity observed following sciatic nerve cuff implantation.
source: These results demonstrate that inhibition of ZI VGAT-positive neurons is sufficient to elicit hypersensitivity in the absence of injury that resembles the hypersensitivity observed following sciatic nerve cuff implantation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claim: The effects of chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons on tactile and pressure sensitivity were transient.
source: The effects of chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons on tactile and pressure sensitivity were transient, as paw withdrawal thresholds in all treated animals returned to pre-injection values 1 day following CNO injections.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claim: Behavioral responses to cold and heat stimulation of the hindpaws were unaltered by chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI in all animals tested.
source: Behavioral responses to cold and heat stimulation of the hindpaws, however, were unaltered by chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI in all animals tested.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claim: Inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI is sufficient to induce hypersensitivity in the absence of injury in a modality-specific manner.
source: Taken together, the results from these chemogenetic experiments demonstrate that inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI is sufficient to induce hypersensitivity in the absence of injury in a modality-specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claim: i.p. injection of CNO resulted in robust c-Fos expression in the ZI of VGAT-cre animals injected with hM3Dq.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4D and i.p. injection of CNO resulted in robust c-Fos expression in the ZI of VGAT-cre animals injected with hM3Dq, compared to the c-Fos expression observed in the ZI of saline-injected control mice that also expressed hM3Dq or CNO-injected control VGAT-cre mice stereotaxically injected with the control virus.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: c-Fos expression in hM3Dq-transduced cells is significantly higher in CNO-treated mice than in saline-treated mice or in mCherry-transduced neurons from CNO-treated mice.
source: Quantification of ZI cells co-expressing c-Fos and mCherry further confirmed that c-Fos expression in hM3Dq-transduced cells is significantly (p<0.05) higher in CNO-treated mice than in saline-treated mice or in mCherry-transduced neurons from CNO-treated mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CNO-mediated activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons led to significant reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation.
source: CNO-mediated activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons led to significant (p<0.0001) reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation, while no measurable effects were seen in saline-injected or CNO-injected mCherry-control mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claim: The effects of activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons were specific to nerve injury.
source: The effects of activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons were specific to nerve injury as withdrawal thresholds in sham-treated mice or the hindpaw contralateral to sciatic nerve cuff were comparable between groups.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claim: Reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity by activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons was modality-specific.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D, reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity was also modality-specific as behavioral responses to cold and heat stimulation of the hindpaws were unaffected by chemogenetic activation of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: Activation of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI reverses cuff-induced pain hypersensitivity in a modality-specific manner.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that activation of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI reverses cuff-induced pain hypersensitivity in a modality-specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claim: Yellow light stimulation significantly inhibited firing responses in NpHR-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in neighboring NpHR-negative neurons.
source: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings of neurons expressing NpHR-mCherry in acute CeA slices confirmed that yellow light (590 nm, 10 mW) stimulation significantly (p<0.0001) inhibited firing responses in NpHR-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in neighboring NpHR-negative neurons (Figure 5E), further validating our experimental approach.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI with yellow light significantly reduced cuff-induced hypersensitivity to pinch stimulation of the treated paw without affecting the untreated paw.
source: At the behavioral level, optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI with yellow light (561 nm, 10 mW) significantly (p<0.0001) reduced cuff-induced hypersensitivity to pinch stimulation of the treated paw without affecting the untreated paw (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Yellow light-mediated behavioral effects were dependent on laser intensity.
source: Yellow light-mediated behavioral effects were dependent on laser intensity, with increasing laser intensities resulting in larger reductions of cuff-induced hypersensitivity at intensities between 0.04 and 0.06 mW, and with a plateau observed at intensities equal to or higher than 0.07 mW (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI resulted in significant reductions of cuff-induced hypersensitivity to tactile, cold, and heat stimulation of the treated hindpaw at both 0.07 mW and 10 mW laser intensities.
source: As illustrated in Figure 6A–D, optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI resulted in significant (p<0.0001) reductions of cuff-induced hypersensitivity to tactile (Figure 6B), cold (Figure 6C), and heat (Figure 6D) stimulation of the treated hindpaw at both 0.07 mW and 10 mW laser intensities.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Injury-induced activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway is necessary for cuff-induced pressure, tactile, and thermal hypersensitivity.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that injury-induced activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway is necessary for cuff-induced pressure, tactile, and thermal hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on optogenetic behavioral data.

claim: Activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons induces bilateral tactile hypersensitivity in the absence of injury.
source: Previous studies have shown that activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons induces bilateral tactile hypersensitivity in the absence of injury Wilson et al., 2019.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Blue light stimulation significantly increased firing responses in ChR2-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in control ChR2-negative neighboring neurons.
source: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings of neurons expressing ChR2-mCherry in acute CeA slices further confirmed that blue light (470 nm, 10 mW) stimulation significantly (P<0.0001) increased firing responses in ChR2-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in control ChR2-negative neighboring neurons (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light significantly increased sensitivity to pinch stimulation of the untreated hindpaw without affecting responses to stimulation of the treated hindpaw.
source: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light (473 nm, 10 mW) significantly (p<0.0001) increased sensitivity to pinch stimulation of the untreated hindpaw without affecting responses to stimulation of the treated hindpaw or responses in PKCδ-cre mice injected with the control-mCherry virus (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Behavioral responses to blue light stimulation are intensity-dependent.
source: Light intensity-response experiments showed that behavioral responses to blue light stimulation are intensity-dependent. Thus, light-induced increases in the sensitivity to pinch of the untreated paw was observed at intensities equal to or higher than 0.6 mW, with a plateau observed starting at 0.8 mW (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light at 0.8 mW or 10 mW significantly increased sensitivity to tactile, cold, and heat stimulation of the untreated hindpaw.
source: Consistent with pinch stimulation results, optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light at 0.8 mW or 10 mW significantly (P<0.01) increased sensitivity to tactile (Figure 8B), cold (Figure 8C), and heat (Figure 8D) stimulation of the untreated hindpaw.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8B-D.

claim: Activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway induces hypersensitivity to tactile, pressure, heat, and cold stimuli in the absence of injury.
source: These results show that activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway induces hypersensitivity to tactile, pressure, heat, and cold stimuli in the absence of injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on optogenetic behavioral data.

claim: Spontaneous ﬁring rates and somatosensory-evoked neuronal responses decrease in the ZI in a rodent model of central pain syndrome.
source: Previous studies have shown that spontaneous ﬁring rates and somatosensory-evoked neuronal responses decrease in the ZI in a rodent model of central pain syndrome (Masri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The present study showed that the ZI receives moderate axonal terminals from CeA-PKCδ neurons.
source: In the present study, we showed that the ZI receives moderate axonal terminals from CeA-PKCδ neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and that inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI contribute to persistent pain-related behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI contribute to persistent pain-related behaviors.
source: In the present study, we showed that the ZI receives moderate axonal terminals from CeA-PKCδ neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and that inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI contribute to persistent pain-related behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons serve as an inhibitory input to the ZI that contributes to the regulation of nociceptive behaviors.
source: It is thus reasonable to postulate that CeA-PKCδ neurons serve as an inhibitory input to the ZI that contributes to the regulation of nociceptive behaviors and provides a mechanistic explanation for the previously reported reductions in ZI activity during pain-related states (Masri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI reduced hypersensitivity to pinch, tactile, cold and heat stimulation.
source: At the behavioral level, we showed that optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI reduced hypersensitivity to pinch, tactile, cold and heat stimulation (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 5-6.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ neurons decreases hypersensitivity to all modalities.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies showing that chemogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ neurons also decreases hypersensitivity to all modalities (Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Thermal modalities are unaffected by chemogenetic manipulations of ZI-VGAT neurons.
source: Notably, however, our experiments also showed that thermal modalities are unaffected by chemogenetic manipulations of ZI-VGAT neurons (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons target a specific subpopulation of ZI neurons that contributes to modulation of all pain modalities.
source: These combined results suggest heterogenous functions of ZI neurons in the modulation of pain-related behaviors, with CeA-PKCδ neurons targeting a specific subpopulation of ZI neurons that contributes to modulation of all pain modalities.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on the combined findings.

claim: ZI is a heterogenous structure that contains multiple cell types.
source: Consistent with this idea, previous studies have shown that ZI is a heterogenous structure that contains multiple cell types (Mitrofanis, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Heterogeneity of function in the CeA has been previously reported.
source: Heterogeneity of function in the CeA has also been previously reported (Kim et al., 2017; Kong and Zweifel, 2021; Moscarello and Penzo, 2022; Venniro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: CeA-PKCδ and somatostatin-positive CeA neurons have opposing functions in the modulation of pain-related responses.
source: In the context of pain, CeA-PKCδ and somatostatin-positive CeA neurons have been shown to have opposing functions in the modulation of pain-related responses (Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons provide inhibitory input to the ventral sector of ZI.
source: Our results indicate that CeA-PKCδ neurons provide inhibitory input to the ventral sector of ZI, and that activation of this inhibitory pathway drives behavioral hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Chemogenetic manipulation of the activity of VGAT-positive ZI neurons bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors in a modality-specific manner.
source: In the present study, we show that chemogenetic manipulation of the activity of VGAT-positive ZI neurons bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors in a modality-specific manner (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: Bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile (but not thermal) stimulation follows inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons in the absence of nerve or tissue injury.
source: Thus, we observe bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile (but not thermal) stimulation following inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons in the absence of nerve or tissue injury (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons reversed nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity to pinch (but not thermal) stimulation.
source: In contrast, chemogenetic activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons reversed nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity to pinch (but not thermal) stimulation (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: Optogenetic activation or inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons influences sensitivity to tactile stimulation.
source: Our results are consistent with previous studies that have shown that optogenetic activation or inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons influences sensitivity to tactile stimulation (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Baseline responses in sham animals or the hindpaw contralateral to sciatic nerve treatment were unaltered by chemogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons in the present study.
source: It is important to note that baseline responses in sham animals or the hindpaw contralateral to sciatic nerve treatment were unaltered by chemogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons in the present study.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Optogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons decreased baseline responses to tactile stimulation in previous studies.
source: This contrasts with previous reports, where optogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons decreased baseline responses to tactile stimulation (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Modulation of behavioral output by optogenetic stimulation is dependent on the frequency and pattern of the stimulation used for the experiments.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that modulation of behavioral output by optogenetic stimulation is dependent on the frequency and pattern of the stimulation used for the experiments (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Deep brain stimulation of zona incerta in human subjects reduced experimental heat pain without affecting mechanical pain thresholds.
source: A recent study further demonstrated that deep brain stimulation of zona incerta in human subjects reduced experimental heat pain without affecting mechanical pain thresholds (Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Both VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons respond to optogenetic stimulation of CeA terminals in the ZI.
source: In the present study, we evaluated the functional contribution of ZI-VGAT neurons to the modulation of pain-related behaviors. Our optogenetic-assisted circuit mapping experiments showed, however, that both VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons respond to optogenetic stimulation of CeA terminals in the ZI (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Somatostatin-positive CeA neurons project to and inhibit parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons.
source: Consistent with these findings, previous studies have shown that CeA neurons, including somatostatin-positive cells, project to and inhibit parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons (Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive neurons in the ZI show an opposite electrophysiological phenotype and function in the modulation of pain-related behaviors than ZI-VGAT neurons.
source: Interestingly, this study demonstrated that parvalbumin-positive neurons in the ZI show an opposite electrophysiological phenotype and function in the modulation of pain-related behaviors than what we and others observe for the ZI-VGAT neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion referencing a previous study.

claim: Inhibition of ZI-VGAT neurons drives behavioral hypersensitivity.
source: Thus, while the present and previous studies show that inhibition of ZI-VGAT neurons drives behavioral hypersensitivity, ablation or silencing of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to be analgesic (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Ablation or silencing of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to be analgesic.
source: Thus, while the present and previous studies show that inhibition of ZI-VGAT neurons drives behavioral hypersensitivity, ablation or silencing of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to be analgesic (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Activation of ZI-VGAT neurons reverses injury-induced hypersensitivity.
source: Similarly, while we and others show that activation of ZI-VGAT neurons reverses injury-induced hypersensitivity, activation of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to promote behavioral hypersensitivity (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Activation of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to promote behavioral hypersensitivity.
source: Similarly, while we and others show that activation of ZI-VGAT neurons reverses injury-induced hypersensitivity, activation of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to promote behavioral hypersensitivity (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons receive inputs from somatostatin-expressing CeA neurons.
source: These combined results are particularly interesting given that parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons receive inputs from somatostatin-expressing CeA neurons (Zhou et al., 2018), which have been previously shown to be inhibited in the context of pain (Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing CeA neurons have been previously shown to be inhibited in the context of pain.
source: These combined results are particularly interesting given that parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons receive inputs from somatostatin-expressing CeA neurons (Zhou et al., 2018), which have been previously shown to be inhibited in the context of pain (Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Injury-induced inhibition of somatostatin-expressing neurons in the CeA disinhibits parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons, resulting in behavioral hypersensitivity.
source: Based on these combined findings, we predict that injury-induced inhibition of somatostatin-expressing neurons in the CeA disinhibits parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons, while injury-induced activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons inhibits a subpopulation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons, both resulting in behavioral hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the discussion based on the combined findings.

claim: Injury-induced activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons inhibits a subpopulation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons, resulting in behavioral hypersensitivity.
source: Based on these combined findings, we predict that injury-induced inhibition of somatostatin-expressing neurons in the CeA disinhibits parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons, while injury-induced activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons inhibits a subpopulation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons, both resulting in behavioral hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the discussion based on the combined findings.
